decks.name: Tumors II: Meningioma, Sellar, Metastases, Skull & Spine (Greenberg)

zeilen: Most common sites together; contralateral leg weakness; SSS invasion decides resectability (do not ligate a patent posterior SSS)
Most easily resected, Simpson I feasible
Anosmia, frontal personality change, Foster Kennedy syndrome; ACA branches pushed posteriorly
Asymmetric visual loss with normal pituitary function; optic canal invasion
Visual loss, ICA/MCA encasement, cavernous sinus invasion; lateral wing tumors often en plaque with proptosis and hyperostosis
Cranial nerve V–VIII deficits, brainstem compression, perforator risk; high morbidity
Mostly anterior/anterolateral; "clockwise" progressive limb weakness, occipital pain, hand atrophy

cards.rueckseite:
- **Incidental, small, asymptomatic:** MRI surveillance (many do not grow, typically < 1–2 mm/yr; calcified tumors grow less)
- **SRS:** small (< 3 cm) residual/recurrent or skull base tumors (cavernous sinus), good local control for grade 1
- **Fractionated RT:** after subtotal resection of grade 2, after any resection of **grade 3**, optic nerve sheath meningioma
- **Grade 2 after GTR:** RT vs. observation still debated
- **Preoperative embolization** for large, hypervascular skull base tumors (best 7–10 days before surgery)

Congenital **large or multiple giant melanocytic nevi** (often over the back, ≥ 20 cm adult size, or ≥ 3 lesions) plus **meningeal melanosis/melanoma** (leptomeningeal melanocytes).
Presents in early childhood with **hydrocephalus**, seizures, raised ICP; associated with **Dandy–Walker** malformation.
MRI: T1-hyperintense foci (amygdala, cerebellum, pons) and leptomeningeal enhancement.
Prognosis poor once symptomatic; malignant transformation common.

cards.vorderseite: CNS germ cell tumors: types and treatment
cards.rueckseite:
- **Germinoma:** radiosensitive; biopsy (often with ETV) → **chemotherapy + reduced-dose RT** (craniospinal or whole-ventricular); > 90% survival
- **Non-germinomatous GCTs** (embryonal carcinoma, **yolk sac** → AFP, **choriocarcinoma** → very high β-hCG and hemorrhage, mixed): chemotherapy + RT, then **second-look surgery** for residual mass
- **Mature teratoma:** surgery alone is curative
- **Growing teratoma syndrome:** mass enlarges during chemotherapy while markers fall → mature teratoma component → resect
- Markers rule out surgery when diagnostic (high AFP/β-hCG); germinomas may have mildly raised β-hCG (syncytiotrophoblasts)

Clonal Langerhans cells (**CD1a**, **langerin/CD207**, S100; Birbeck granules; **BRAF V600E** often); 70% under 20 years.
**Skull:** tender enlarging lump; X-ray: round **punched-out** lytic lesion with **beveled edges**, no sclerotic rim; "button sequestrum".
**CNS:** hypothalamic–pituitary region → **diabetes insipidus**, thickened stalk; neurodegenerative leukoencephalopathy.
Hand–Schüller–Christian triad: skull lesions, DI, exophthalmos.
**Treatment:** solitary skull lesion → curettage/excision (or steroid injection); multisystem → chemotherapy (vinblastine/prednisone), BRAF inhibitors.

cards.titel: Knosp grading (cavernous sinus invasion by pituitary tumors)
zeilen: Lateral extent relative to the ICA (coronal MRI)
Does not reach the medial tangent between the intracavernous and supraclinoid ICA
Beyond the medial tangent, not past the intercarotid line (centers of the ICA)
Beyond the intercarotid line, not past the lateral tangent
Beyond the lateral tangent, into the superior (3A) or inferior (3B) cavernous compartment
Total encasement of the intracavernous ICA
cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 52.7, p. 884. Grades 3–4 = true invasion; gross total resection becomes unlikely (3B and 4 worst).

cards.rueckseite:
- **Prolactin** (dilute the sample if a large tumor has a low value → **hook effect**)
- **IGF-1** (best screen for acromegaly; GH itself is pulsatile)
- **8 AM cortisol** ± ACTH; 24-h urinary free cortisol / late-night salivary cortisol / 1 mg dexamethasone test if Cushing suspected
- **TSH and free T4** (low/normal TSH with low T4 = central hypothyroidism)
- **LH, FSH**, testosterone/estradiol
- Serum Na and osmolality (DI)
- Formal **visual fields** and acuity

The only pituitary tumor with **medical first-line therapy** (dopamine agonist, **cabergoline** preferred: more effective, better tolerated).
- PRL **> 500 ng/mL:** surgical normalization unlikely → medical therapy first; response expected within 4–6 weeks
- **Surgery:** dopamine agonist intolerance or resistance, apoplexy, CSF leak, cystic tumors, patient preference (microadenoma)
- **Pregnancy:** symptomatic growth in < 3% of microadenomas vs. **≈ 30% of macroadenomas** → follow visual fields
- Dopamine agonist shrinkage of invasive tumors can cause **CSF rhinorrhea**; prolonged bromocriptine may cause fibrosis and lower surgical cure
- Cabergoline at high doses: cardiac valve fibrosis

**Diagnosis:** elevated age-adjusted **IGF-1**; confirm with **failure of GH suppression < 1 ng/mL** after a 75 g oral glucose load.
**Morbidity:** cardiomyopathy, hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnea, colon polyps, arthropathy, carpal tunnel → reduced life expectancy.
**Treatment:** **transsphenoidal surgery** first; then somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide, pasireotide), **pegvisomant** (GH-receptor antagonist: normalizes IGF-1 in ≈ 97%, tumor size unchanged), cabergoline, radiotherapy/SRS.
**Cure:** normal IGF-1 and GH < 1 ng/mL after glucose.

After biochemical Cushing syndrome with **ACTH-dependent** pattern: MRI (microadenoma often invisible) and **inferior petrosal sinus sampling** with CRH/desmopressin (central:peripheral ACTH ratio ≥ 2 basal or ≥ 3 after stimulation = pituitary source; lateralization unreliable).
**Treatment:** transsphenoidal resection; **postoperative cortisol nadir < 2–5 mcg/dL** predicts remission (patients need replacement). Failures: repeat surgery, RT/SRS, medication (ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat, pasireotide), **bilateral adrenalectomy**.

Follows **10–30% of bilateral adrenalectomies** for Cushing disease: loss of cortisol feedback lets the corticotroph adenoma grow.
**Triad:** **hyperpigmentation** (earliest sign; ACTH/MSH), markedly elevated ACTH, enlarging pituitary tumor (can be aggressive, invade the cavernous sinus).
**Treatment:** transsphenoidal or transcranial surgery, radiation/SRS, medication.

Rare (< 1–2%); **central hyperthyroidism:** elevated free T4/T3 with **normal or high TSH** (inappropriately unsuppressed), elevated α-subunit.
Often **large and invasive** at diagnosis (many previously treated with thyroid ablation, which removes feedback).
**Treatment:** render euthyroid preoperatively (somatostatin analog ± antithyroid drugs, β-blocker), then transsphenoidal surgery; somatostatin analogs or RT for residual tumor.

cards.vorderseite: After transsphenoidal surgery: DI watch and delayed hyponatremia
cards.rueckseite:
- Strict intake/output hourly, urine specific gravity, Na every 6 h
- **DI criteria:** urine output **> 250 mL/h for 2 h** with **specific gravity < 1.005**
- Steroid coverage until the axis is tested (always in Cushing disease)
- No straws, nose blowing or incentive spirometry (CSF leak)
- **Delayed hyponatremia (SIADH) ≈ day 5–10** (peak around day 7) → check Na about 1 week after discharge; mild fluid restriction
- Remember the triphasic response

- **CSF leak** (most common serious one; risk higher with intraoperative leak, extended approaches) → meningitis
- **Carotid artery injury** (cavernous/paraclival ICA): pack, control BP, then angiography (pseudoaneurysm, CCF) → endovascular treatment
- Hypopituitarism, **DI**, SIADH
- Visual worsening (hematoma in the tumor bed, overpacking, chiasmal prolapse into an empty sella)
- Epistaxis (sphenopalatine artery), sinusitis, anosmia, septal perforation
- Mortality < 1%

cards.vorderseite: Posterior pituitary tumors (pituicytoma, granular cell tumor, spindle cell oncocytoma)
cards.rueckseite:
Low-grade (CNS WHO grade 1) tumors of the **neurohypophysis/infundibulum** (TTF-1 positive) in adults; mimic nonfunctioning macroadenomas.
Key surgical point: they are **highly vascular and firm**, often adherent to the stalk/hypothalamus → bleeding, subtotal resection, postoperative DI more common.
Presentation: visual loss, hypopituitarism, mild hyperprolactinemia (stalk effect).

Leptomeningeal spread in ≈ 5–8% of systemic cancers: **breast, lung, melanoma**, leukemia/lymphoma; also primary CNS tumors (medulloblastoma, ependymoma, GBM).
**Clinic:** multifocal signs at several levels: cranial nerve palsies, radiculopathies, headache, hydrocephalus, confusion.
**Diagnosis:** contrast MRI of brain and **entire spine** (before LP); CSF cytology positive in ≈ 50% on the first LP, ≈ 90% after **three** LPs (high volume, rapid processing); high protein, low glucose.
**Treatment:** palliative: RT to bulky/symptomatic sites, intrathecal chemotherapy (via **Ommaya reservoir**), systemic agents, shunt for hydrocephalus. Median survival weeks to months.

zeilen: Beyond the sinuses (orbit, skull base, intracranial, cervical nodes, metastases)
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 935–937. Arises from olfactory epithelium (cribriform plate), bimodal age peaks; presents with nasal obstruction, epistaxis, anosmia; "dumbbell" mass across the cribriform plate. Treatment: craniofacial or endoscopic endonasal resection + RT.

cards.rueckseite:
Incidental in ≈ 1–4% of MRIs (up to 40% at autopsy); young women.
Typical: < 1–1.5 cm, CSF-like or slightly T1/FLAIR hyperintense, **thin rim enhancement**, no solid nodule.
Usually asymptomatic → **no routine follow-up** if typical (or one follow-up scan).
**Surgery** only for hydrocephalus, Parinaud syndrome, growth or atypical features (nodular enhancement → consider pineocytoma); rare **pineal apoplexy**.

Sella filled with CSF because the diaphragma sellae is incompetent and the gland is flattened.
- **Primary:** obese, hypertensive middle-aged women; associated with **idiopathic intracranial hypertension**; usually asymptomatic, pituitary function generally normal (mild hyperprolactinemia), rarely CSF rhinorrhea
- **Secondary:** after surgery, radiation, apoplexy or bromocriptine shrinkage; can cause **chiasmal herniation** with visual loss (chiasmapexy)

No treatment unless symptomatic.

cards.vorderseite: Modified Dandy criteria for idiopathic intracranial hypertension
cards.rueckseite:
1. Signs and symptoms of raised ICP (headache, papilledema, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations)
2. **No localizing signs** except VI palsy
3. Awake and alert
4. **Normal imaging** (no mass, no hydrocephalus, no venous sinus thrombosis on MRV)
5. **Opening pressure > 25 cm H₂O** (lateral decubitus, relaxed) with **normal CSF** composition
6. No other cause

MRI signs: empty sella, flattened posterior globe, distended optic nerve sheaths, **transverse sinus stenosis**. For refractory cases with a pressure gradient: **venous sinus stenting**.

zeilen: Most common primary bone tumor of the calvaria; dense, outer table, sinus (frontal); Gardner syndrome if multiple
Expanded diploë, **honeycomb/sunburst** trabeculae, "spoke-wheel"; resect with margin of normal bone
Lytic lesion with a **sclerotic rim**, diploic expansion
Punched-out lytic lesion, **beveled edges**, no sclerotic rim, tender
**Ground-glass** expansion; McCune–Albright (polyostotic + café-au-lait + precocious puberty); optic canal narrowing
Bilateral inner table thickening of the frontal bone, older women, harmless (vs. meningioma: unilateral)
Osteoporosis circumscripta (lytic), later cotton-wool skull; basilar invagination, hearing loss

cards.text: Spinal tumors by compartment: **extradural** {{c1::≈ 55%}} (mostly metastases), **intradural extramedullary** {{c2::≈ 40%}} (meningioma, schwannoma), **intramedullary** {{c3::≈ 5%}} (ependymoma, astrocytoma, hemangioblastoma). Myelography sign of an IDEM tumor: {{c4::meniscus (cap) sign with widening of the ipsilateral subarachnoid space}}.

zeilen: Can be aggressive, recurs; rare malignant change
NSAIDs, CT-guided **RF ablation** or excision of the nidus
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 990–991. CT: lucent nidus with surrounding sclerosis; intense uptake on bone scan.

cards.rueckseite:
Most common benign spinal tumor (≈ 10% at autopsy), usually incidental.
**Imaging:** vertical **"corduroy"** striations (X-ray/sagittal CT), **"polka-dot"** on axial CT; T1 and T2 bright (fat).
**Aggressive hemangioma** (rare, thoracic, T1 hypointense, extends into the canal/soft tissue, pregnancy) → cord compression.
**Treatment of symptomatic/aggressive:** **preoperative embolization** or vertebroplasty (ethanol injection), decompression, radiation.

cards.vorderseite: Giant cell tumor and aneurysmal bone cyst of the spine
cards.rueckseite:
**Giant cell tumor:** young adults (20–40), **sacrum** and vertebral bodies; lytic, expansile, no matrix; locally aggressive, high recurrence, rare lung metastases. Treatment: **en bloc** or intralesional resection, **denosumab** (RANKL inhibitor), embolization, RT for unresectable.
**Aneurysmal bone cyst:** children/adolescents, posterior elements, expansile with **fluid–fluid levels**; may be secondary to GCT/osteoblastoma. Treatment: embolization, curettage/resection, sclerotherapy, denosumab.
